definition: In data analysis, anomaly detection (also referred to as outlier detection and sometimes as novelty detection) is generally understood to be the identification of rare items, events or observations which deviate significantly from the majority of the data and do not conform to a well defined notion of normal behavior.
details: Such examples may arouse suspicions of being generated by a different mechanism, or appear inconsistent with the remainder of that set of data. Anomaly detection finds application in many domains including cybersecurity, medicine, machine vision, statistics, neuroscience, law enforcement and financial fraud to name only a few. Anomalies were initially searched for clear rejection or omission from the data to aid statistical analysis, for example to compute the mean or standard deviation. They were also removed to better predictions from models such as linear regression, and more recently their removal aids the performance of machine learning algorithms. However, in many applications anomalies themselves are of interest and are the observations most desirous in the entire data set, which need to be identified and separated from noise or irrelevant outliers. Three broad categories of anomaly detection techniques exist: Supervised anomaly detection techniques require a data set that has been labeled as "normal" and "abnormal" and involves training a classifier. However, this approach is rarely used in anomaly detection due to the general unavailability of labelled data and the inherent unbalanced nature of the classes. Semi-supervised anomaly detection techniques assume that some portion of the data is labelled. This may be any combination of the normal or anomalous data, but more often than not, the techniques construct a model representing normal behavior from a given normal training data set, and then test the likelihood of a test instance to be generated by the model. Unsupervised anomaly detection techniques assume the data is unlabelled and are by far the most commonly used due to their wider and relevant application.

explainer.lead: Anomaly detection looks for observations or patterns that depart substantially from what is normal in a particular setting. It helps people find events worth attention, such as fraud, equipment failure, or a security intrusion, without assuming that every unusual observation is an error.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a basket of red apples and noticing one bright blue apple. Anomaly detection is the job of noticing things that do not fit, while remembering that the blue apple might be a mistake, a rare find, or something important. What counts as strange can also depend on the situation: a coat is normal in winter but surprising on a hot summer day.
tiers.practitioner: Unsupervised methods are the most commonly used because labelled anomalies are often unavailable, while supervised classification requires normal and abnormal labels and must handle class imbalance. A typical pipeline fits a model of normality, produces an anomaly score, and applies a threshold to make a binary decision; intrusion-detection systems can use thresholds and statistics, soft computing, or inductive learning. Take care with context, noise, and irrelevant outliers, and model relationships explicitly for time series, spatial data, sequences, and graphs when contextual or collective anomalies matter.
tiers.paperLevel: Given observations x_i and a fitted model N of normality, a method commonly computes an anomaly score s(x_i; N) and labels x_i anomalous when s(x_i; N) exceeds a decision threshold τ. Normality may be characterized through probability distributions, distances or local densities, clusters, boundaries, prediction errors, or reconstruction errors. There is no single operational definition across domains, so results depend on the data representation, context, model assumptions, and decision rule. Anomaly detection for intrusion-detection systems was proposed by Dorothy Denning in 1986.

explainer.example: A bank models normal transaction behavior and scores each new transaction by its departure from that model. An unusually large transaction receives a score above the chosen threshold and is flagged for fraud review; the flag identifies it for attention rather than proving that fraud occurred.

usedIn.name: Intrusion detection
usedIn.detail: Profiles of users, workstations, networks, hosts, and programs can reveal activity associated with security intrusions.

usedIn.name: Fintech fraud detection
usedIn.detail: Unusual transactions or patterns of activity can be flagged for fraud prevention.

usedIn.name: Video surveillance
usedIn.detail: Methods using CNNs and SRUs can analyze video feeds for activities or behaviors that deviate from normal patterns.

usedIn.name: System health monitoring
usedIn.detail: Departures from normal behavior can support fault detection and event detection in sensor networks.

explainer.intuition: First describe what normal behavior looks like, then measure how far each observation or pattern departs from it. Anomalies can be single points, observations unusual only in a particular context, or collections that are unusual only when considered together.
howItWorks: Choose the observations, context, and representation that define the setting.
Fit a model of normality using labelled, partly labelled, or unlabelled data.
Measure departures using criteria such as distance, density, probability, or reconstruction error.
Convert each departure into a numerical anomaly score.
Apply a decision threshold and separate flagged anomalies from noise or irrelevant outliers.
explainer.whyItMatters: The observations that deviate from normal behavior are sometimes the most valuable ones in a dataset, revealing fraud, failures, intrusions, or other events of interest. Removing unwanted anomalies can also improve statistics such as the mean and standard deviation, data visualisation, and supervised-learning accuracy.
misconceptions: An anomaly is not necessarily a data error; it can also be a valid rare observation or an important event.
Rarity or distance from other observations alone does not define every anomaly.
A high anomaly score is not an automatic label until a decision threshold is applied.
